methodological_rigor.justification: The manuscript develops and validates a new sequencing-based assay (BIVID-MaP) by explicitly testing mechanistic requirements for RT deletions, including the combination of VQ covalent modification chemistry with TGIRT versus SuperScript IV and a low-reactivity VQ (SMe) control to show dependence on covalent modification rather than binding alone (Results: Fig. 1; Results text). It demonstrates versatility across different RNA-binding small molecules (berberine and CMA for G4s; SMN-C2 for a hairpin loop) and provides orthogonal validation using affinity-selection mass spectrometry and G4-focused biophysical assays (CD spectra and NMM fluorescence) when interpreting variant effects (Results: Figs. 3–4; Discussion). The methods are detailed enough to reproduce key steps (library design from ONGene/TSGene/MANE, COSMIC variant collection, in vitro transcription, reaction conditions, and RT/deep sequencing workflow), and it reports replicate structure for major readouts (e.g., BIVID-MaP n = 2 independent experiments; AS-MS and fluorescence assays with multiple independent experiments) (Methods; Fig. 3–4 legends). Remaining limitations are that several quantitative comparisons rely on small n for sequencing-based measures (often n = 2) and the manuscript does not present power calculations or a prespecified statistical analysis plan beyond per-assay tests reported in figure legends (Fig. 3 legend; Methods/Results).

clinical_relevance_loe.justification: This is a basic science/method development study that introduces a platform (BIVID-MaP) to map variant-specific RNA-small molecule interactions and applies it to a 5' UTR somatic mutation library derived from cancer-associated variants (Abstract; Methods: COSMIC/ONGene/TSGene; Results). On the Oxford CEBM hierarchy, the design does not include patient outcomes or interventional clinical data, so it maps to LoE 5. Clinically, the relevance is indirect but plausible: the method addresses a concrete drug-discovery gap by enabling discrimination of binding differences driven by single-nucleotide variants, which the authors motivate with examples of variant-dependent pharmacologic effects and RNA-targeting drug development needs (Introduction; Discussion). However, the work stops at in vitro/lysate demonstrations and binding/structure assays rather than showing therapeutic impact or biomarker-guided treatment in patients, so translational immediacy is moderate (Results; Discussion).

reporting_quality.justification: No single clinical or animal reporting checklist cleanly applies because the manuscript is primarily a chemical biology / sequencing-methods study, so the most appropriate designation is "other" (Methods/Results). Reporting is strong for key experimental components: reagent choices and conditions for modification reactions, RT enzyme comparisons, library construction, and variant library provenance (COSMIC; MANE; UCSC/GENCODE) are described in a stepwise manner (Methods). The results and figure legends report replicate counts and statistical tests for validation assays (e.g., Welch's t-tests with P-values in AS-MS and NMM fluorescence; BIVID-MaP performed in two independent experiments) and explicitly discuss methodological limitations such as overlap between deletion sites and variant positions and U-bias of VQ chemistry (Fig. 3–4 legends; Discussion). The manuscript repeatedly references "Source data" and provides extensive Supplementary Data tables for sequences/templates, supporting higher reproducibility even though analysis code availability is not explicitly described in the normalized text (Methods: Supplementary Data; Fig. 3–4 legends; Additional Sections: Source data).

novelty_literature.justification: The core novelty is the introduction of BIVID-MaP as a variant-resolving, high-throughput strategy to detect RNA-small molecule interactions by leveraging binding-dependent covalent modification and TGIRT-specific RT deletion signatures, explicitly addressing the stated technical barrier that prior RT-stop and substitution-based MaP approaches could not resolve variant-specific interactions at scale (Abstract; Introduction; Results). The approach is not just an incremental assay tweak: it changes the readout modality (RT deletions) to preserve sequence information for SNV attribution and reduces false positives compared with substitution-based signals in repetitive regions, as argued and supported in the Discussion. Applying the method to a cancer-derived 5' UTR somatic mutation library and finding mutations that increase or decrease binding, with orthogonal validation (AS-MS; CD/NMM), demonstrates a new capability rather than only a proof-of-concept on a single RNA (Results: Figs. 3–4). The authors also articulate clear extensions and current limitations (overlapping deletion/variant sites; U-selectivity of VQ), which strengthens the novelty claim by defining the contribution boundary (Discussion).

writing_presentation.justification: The manuscript communicates a clear problem statement (variant-specific RNA-ligand interactions) and logically progresses from mechanistic discovery of RT deletions, to method validation across ligands/structures, and then to library-scale application with orthogonal validation assays (Introduction; Results; Discussion). Methods provide concrete procedural detail (buffers, concentrations, reaction times, library design sources, and simulation setup), which supports reproducibility and reader comprehension (Methods). Figure captions (as preserved) are information-dense and include replicate counts and statistical testing, which helps interpretability in the absence of actual images in this normalized corpus (Figures section excerpts). Some sections are technically dense with heavy acronym load (e.g., chemistry/linker design and sequencing workflow), but the narrative generally remains coherent and well structured (Methods/Results).

key_strengths: Clear technical innovation: binding-dependent covalent modification plus TGIRT-driven RT deletion profiling enables variant-specific RNA-small molecule interaction mapping with retained SNV information (Abstract; Results Fig. 1; Discussion).
Strong control structure supports mechanism (TGIRT vs SSIV; reactive VQ vs low-reactive VQ; time-dependence) and reduces alternative explanations for the deletion signal (Results; Discussion).
Demonstrated generality across different ligands and RNA structure classes and scaled to a cancer-derived 5' UTR somatic mutation library (Results; Methods: COSMIC/ONGene/TSGene design).
Orthogonal validation with AS-MS and G4-supporting assays (CD spectra and NMM fluorescence) strengthens interpretation of variant-specific binding differences (Results/Figs. 3–4; Discussion).
key_concerns: Several key sequencing-based quantitative comparisons use small replicate counts (often n = 2 for BIVID-MaP), which limits precision for effect-size estimation across many variants (Fig. 3–4 legends; Results).

The chemistry has an acknowledged base bias (VQ selectivity for U) and can miss interactions in U-depleted sequences, constraining general applicability without further modifier development (Discussion).
Variants cannot be distinguished when RT deletions overlap the variant site, requiring secondary assays; this is a practical limitation for some SNV contexts (Discussion).
The work is translationally motivated but remains preclinical/in vitro/lysate-based; no patient-level functional consequence of variant-specific binding is demonstrated (Introduction; Discussion).
chief_reviewer.rationale: This is a high-quality, clearly motivated methods paper with strong mechanistic controls and convincing orthogonal validation; modest replicate depth for some sequencing comparisons and chemistry/interpretation edge cases are best addressed as minor revisions at a Tier 2 venue.
